analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans that cover pregnancy to also cover infertility treatment, including IVF.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote in the 110th Congress and died when the session ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any employer or individual health plan that covers pregnancy care to also cover treatment for infertility — including fertility drugs, insemination, and in vitro fertilization — with the same cost-sharing as other services. It would have applied to private group plans, individual insurance, federal employees' coverage, and military health plans [S2] [S3]. Plans could not dodge the rule by dropping people or paying providers not to offer treatment [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People with infertility — the bill's findings cite more than 6 million American women and men, about 10 percent of the reproductive-age population — plus federal employees and military families, who would no longer pay the full cost of IVF and related treatment out of pocket [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Plans covering obstetrical services must cover infertility treatment chosen by the patient and doctor, including ovulation induction, insemination, IVF, and related procedures, with cost-sharing no worse than for similar services [S2] [S3].
Coverage extends to the individual market, Federal Employees Health Benefit plans, and Defense Department health plans, so federal workers and military families are included [S2] [S3].
Plans are barred from dropping enrollees, offering them cash incentives to skip treatment, penalizing providers, or blocking doctors from discussing options in order to avoid the mandate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and premium-payers behind group plans, who would absorb the cost of a new covered benefit spread across all enrollees; fertility treatment such as IVF is among the more expensive services in medicine.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and all premium payers

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises premiums for everyone in covered plans, including people who will never need fertility care, since the bill forbids plans from imposing higher cost-sharing on infertility treatment than on similar services [S3].

Even supporters would concede the benefit is bounded: assisted reproduction is covered only after cheaper treatments fail, with a lifetime cap of 6 egg retrievals, so the mandate controls costs but also limits care for some patients [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 10 percent of the reproductive-age population facing infertility, a benefit that covers IVF — which typically costs thousands of dollars per cycle out of pocket — is substantial. The cost is real but diffuse: somewhat higher premiums spread across all enrollees in group and individual plans. The bill's limits on how many attempts are covered, and its requirement to try cheaper treatments first, are designed to keep that cost down, at the price of leaving some patients short of the care they need.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees and two health subcommittees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Anthony Weiner introduced the bill on June 27, 2007, joined by Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz [S1] [S3].

It was referred to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Oversight and Government Reform, and Armed Services — and then to the Health subcommittee in June 2007 and the Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions subcommittee in September 2007 [S5].
No further action was taken; no committee vote, floor vote, or Senate companion action appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers came out ahead: they never had to add infertility coverage to plans. Couples with infertility gained nothing and continued to pay fertility treatment costs out of pocket.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers spared the mandate

for.name: Rep. Anthony Weiner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Family Building Act of 2007 and recruited cosponsors.

against.name: House committees of jurisdiction
against.role: Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Oversight and Government Reform, and Armed Services
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee and subcommittee for over a year without a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split is untested; all 20 named supporters in the record, the sponsor and 19 cosponsors, were Democrats [S4].

industries.note: The bill forces plans and issuers offering group, individual, federal employee, and military coverage to add an expensive new benefit and forbids the workarounds insurers commonly use to shed such mandates, such as higher cost-sharing for the targeted service [S2] [S3]. Its death left insurers free to keep excluding or limiting fertility coverage.

industries.industry: Fertility clinics and reproductive medicine providers
industries.note: A coverage mandate would make insurers the paying channel for IVF and related treatment, turning millions of currently self-pay patients into covered ones. The bill also requires covered treatment at facilities meeting American Society for Reproductive Medicine standards, favoring established clinics [S3].
Group plans, including collectively bargained ones after transition, would have to add the benefit, raising employers' benefit costs; employees would share through premiums.
